title: Air India Crash Probe Enters Final Phase With Psychological Autopsy, Report Due October
excerpt: India's AAIB has prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy as it moves into the analysis stage of the Ahmedabad disaster investigation, a Supreme Court filing reveals.
body:
• India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has conducted a psychological autopsy and prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript as part of its probe into the June 2025 Air India crash that killed 260 people.
  • The AAIB told the Supreme Court the investigation is in its analysis phase and expects to complete remaining activities within six weeks, with a draft final report likely by October.
  • The bureau opposes petitions for a parallel judicial probe and the release of cockpit voice recordings, citing absolute statutory prohibitions under the 2025 investigation rules.
  • The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board will receive the draft report for review before it is finalised and published.

India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has conducted a psychological autopsy and prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript as it enters the final stages of its probe into the Air India Flight AI-171 crash, according to a court filing made before the Supreme Court this week.

The filing, dated Tuesday, did not identify whose psychological autopsy was conducted or disclose any findings on the crash of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner that killed 260 people shortly after takeoff from Ahmedabad on June 12, 2025, according to Reuters.

Investigation Progress and Remaining Steps

The AAIB said the probe has moved into its analysis phase, with findings and conclusions being drawn across operational, technical, human-factors and organisational areas. Investigators have interviewed Air India 787 pilots, crew members who had previously flown with the pilots of the crashed aircraft, technical personnel who prepared the jet, air traffic controllers, weather officials and human-factors specialists.

An analysis of data retrieved in late May from an engine monitoring unit is still awaited, and an assessment of certain organisational factors remains in progress, the bureau said. Families of the flight crew were approached at their residences during the early stages of the investigation.

The AAIB expects remaining investigation activities to be completed within approximately six weeks, subject to pending "external dependencies." A draft final report is expected around October, after which it will be circulated to relevant participating countries for comment before being finalised and published. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board is among the parties due to receive the draft.

Supreme Court Battle Over Transparency

The court filing came as the AAIB pushed back against petitions seeking an independent judicial probe and access to cockpit voice recordings. Among the petitioners are Pushkaraj Sabharwal, the father of deceased pilot Captain Sumeet Sabharwal, and the Federation of Indian Pilots, who have sought a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge to conduct what they call a "fair, transparent and technically robust" investigation.

"These protections serve a critical purpose: they preserve the candour of witnesses, the independence of investigators, the integrity of the no-blame investigation process."

— AAIB, in its counter affidavit to the Supreme Court

The AAIB argued that Rule 17(5) of the Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2025 imposes an "absolute statutory prohibition" on disclosing cockpit voice recordings and airborne image recordings to the public. Only the Central Government can decide whether protected investigation material should be released, and no such decision has been taken, the bureau said.

The Safety Matters Foundation has also filed a petition seeking a court-monitored inquiry, raising concerns about the composition of the AAIB investigation team. It contends that several team members are from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, which is itself under scrutiny in relation to the crash.

The Pilot's Father and the Fuel Cutoff Question

The disclosures in the court filing were prompted by a lawsuit filed by Pushkar Raj Sabharwal after an AAIB home visit last year upset him. He said officials implied his son cut the fuel supply to the plane's engines after takeoff. According to U.S. officials' early assessment reported by Reuters last year, the cockpit recording of dialogue between the two pilots supported the view that the captain cut the flow of fuel to the engines.

The AAIB said media speculation and narratives attributing blame to the pilots had caused some witnesses to become "restrictive and non-responsive," complicating the investigation.

What Happened on June 12, 2025

The London-bound Boeing 787 Dreamliner crashed into the BJ Medical College hostel complex in Ahmedabad less than a minute after takeoff. It killed 241 of the 242 people on board and 19 others on the ground. India's preliminary report, released in July 2025, detailed that the aircraft's engine fuel cutoff switches transitioned from "RUN" to "CUTOFF" position one after another within one second of each other, just as the jet reached its maximum airspeed of 180 knots during takeoff.

One pilot was recorded asking the other why he cut off the fuel, with the other responding that he had not, according to the cockpit voice recording.

What Comes Next

The AAIB has urged the Supreme Court to dismiss the writ petitions, arguing the statutory and treaty framework under the Chicago Convention and ICAO Annex 13 constitutes a "complete code" that leaves no legal basis for a parallel investigation. The bureau maintains that the purpose of the probe is solely to improve aviation safety and prevent future accidents, not to apportion blame or determine liability.

If the six-week timeline holds, the AAIB's analysis phase would conclude by late August, setting the stage for the draft final report to be circulated internationally before a final version is published. The findings will be closely watched by families of the victims, aviation regulators worldwide and Boeing, which faces scrutiny over yet another 787 incident.
image_caption: Air India aircraft parked on the tarmac at an Indian airport. The AAIB is in the final stages of its investigation into the June 2025 crash of an Air India Boeing 787 Dreamliner in Ahmedabad that killed 260 people.
nri_angle: The Ahmedabad crash killed passengers on a London-bound flight, and many victims had ties to the Indian diaspora in the UK; the investigation's outcome will affect international aviation safety standards for routes connecting India to diaspora hubs.
